did_you_know.text: Did you know? The laws of impurity in this chapter were meant to preserve the holiness of the Israelite camp, which symbolized God's dwelling place among them.
Did you know? The expulsion of the impure from the camp applied to both men and women, emphasizing that holiness and purity were required of every individual in Israel.
Did you know? One who committed a "ma'al" (trespass) was required to fully return what was taken, plus an additional fifth (20%) of its value as a penalty and atonement.
Did you know? If the wronged person had no "goel" (next of kin who could receive payment), the restitution was given to the priests, highlighting their role as representatives of divine justice.
Did you know? The jealousy offering was made of simple barley flour without oil or frankincense, unlike many other offerings, to symbolize poverty, distress, and lack of joy.
Did you know? Mixing dust from the Tabernacle floor with the bitter water symbolized the earth as a witness and the holiness of the place where divine judgment would occur.
Did you know? Uncovering a woman's head in public was a highly shaming act in ancient culture, symbolizing the revelation of her secret and loss of honor.

Did you know? The priest wrote the curse words on a scroll and then dissolved them into the water, a rare act where God's name was erased, so that the curse would mystically transfer its power into the drink.

Did you know? The physical results of the curse – "swelling belly and falling thigh" – are usually interpreted as divinely induced miscarriage or infertility, emphasizing the severity of punishment for infidelity.
Did you know? If the woman was found innocent, the ritual not only cleared her name but also promised her a blessing of fertility, a highly desired outcome in ancient society.
